title: Patio string lights
topic: A friend counts poles for string lights around a closed patio perimeter
blurb: 40 feet divided by 8 is 5 poles — sounds like a classic forgotten end-post.
prompt: A friend texted this on the way to the hardware store. Tap a line if their count is off, or call it clean.

segments.label: The loop
segments.text: Hanging café lights all the way around our square backyard patio — 40 feet of perimeter, closing back into the same outlet corner.

segments.label: The spacing
segments.text: I want a pole every 8 feet along the edge so the wire doesn't sag.

segments.label: The count
segments.text: 40 divided by 8 is 5, so I'm grabbing 5 poles at the hardware store.

segments.label: The run
segments.text: Heading out now before they close.

conclusion: 40 feet around the patio with a pole every 8 feet means 5 poles.

diagnosis: A 40-foot square patio has 10-foot sides, so the perimeter can't close back neatly at the outlet corner.
String lights sag between poles, so you actually need more than 40 feet of perimeter cable.
Closing back to the same corner means the outlet corner needs two separate poles for start and end.
A square has four corners, so any spacing has to divide 10 feet evenly to stay on the edges.
fix: Leave one side open so the lights run straight instead of looping back.
Put two poles at the outlet corner so the start and end clips don't collide.
Measure each 10-foot side individually instead of using the 40-foot total.
Buy a 48-foot string so the sag doesn't pull the loop short.

diagnosis: Because each side of the square is 10 feet, placing poles every 8 feet forces them off the four corners, so you'll need extra corner poles.
8 feet is too wide for café lights; the wire needs a pole every 5 feet or it will sag.
You can't space poles by 8 feet around a square without changing the total perimeter.
Measuring every 8 feet along the edge ignores the diagonal distance at each turn.
fix: Change the spacing to 10 feet so every pole lands cleanly on a corner.
Add 4 extra corner poles on top of the 8-foot spacing poles.
Switch to 5-foot spacing so every 10-foot side gets an exact whole number of spans.
Place poles at the four corners first, then fill in the midpoints.

diagnosis: Classic off-by-one: 5 gaps of 8 feet require 6 poles, because you have to count both the starting pole and the ending pole.
40 divided by 8 gives 5 intervals, so you need 4 poles between the corners plus 4 corner poles — 8 total.
Because 8 doesn't divide a 10-foot side evenly, you need to round up per side (2 poles × 4 sides = 8 poles).
With 5 poles around 40 feet, the gaps between poles stretch out to 10 feet each, not 8.
fix: Grab 6 poles (40 ÷ 8 + 1) so you don't come up one pole short at the end.
Grab 8 poles — 2 for each 10-foot side — so every turn is supported.
Grab 4 poles for the four corners and accept 10-foot spans.
Grab 7 poles so both ends of the wire and every gap are covered.

diagnosis: Heading out now with 5 poles means a second trip back tomorrow for the missing sixth pole.
You forgot to count hooks and zip ties, so 5 poles won't be enough to finish tonight.

fix: Buy 6 poles while you're already at the store so you don't make a second run.
Sketch the four 10-foot sides first and buy 8 poles instead.
Pick up an extra pole for the outlet corner just in case.
Wait until tomorrow and measure the corner posts before buying.
